title: BalancerPoolerV2.migrateMint emits no contract-level event; off-chain reconstruction must infer migration intent from the (ClaimBurned, N x ClaimMintedFor) emission pattern on NFTMinterV2
description:
migrateMint emits no event of its own. The only on-chain trace is the byproduct emission from NFTMinterV2: one ClaimBurned(holder=msg.sender, tokenId=4, quantity=amount) plus `amount` separate ClaimMintedFor(recipient=mintRecipient, dispatcherIndex=6, minter=address(this)) events. Off-chain indexers / accounting systems that need to distinguish 'this user migrated via migrateMint' from 'this user burned id-4 via some other authorized burner and an unrelated authorized minter happened to mint N id-6 to the same recipient' have to perform a structural match against the byproduct emissions: same tx hash, ClaimBurned amount==N, N adjacent ClaimMintedFor with the same caller and recipient. The match works today because the BalancerPoolerV2 is the only authorized burner for id-4 and the only path that calls both burn and mintFor in one tx — but the invariant is implicit, not enforced, and any future authorized-burner or authorized-minter (the project is explicit that more will be added) breaks the off-chain reconstruction without warning.

This also makes on-chain rate-limiting infeasible: any consumer contract that wants to react to 'a migration happened' (e.g., an off-chain rewards distributor crediting migrators, an on-chain cooldown contract, a per-user migration cap) must register either a CalimBurned or ClaimMintedFor handler and then match the structural pattern itself. A first-class MigrationCompleted event on the dispatcher would let downstream consumers subscribe directly and is the standard pattern.

Spec-vs-implementation also: the docstring on the function describes the behaviour ('Burn `amount` of id-4 NFTs from msg.sender and mint `amount` of id-6 NFTs to `mintRecipient`'), but no event documents the (caller, mintRecipient, amount) tuple. Reorg-aware indexers ordinarily key off function-level events; here they have to special-case the emission pattern.
exploit_path:
Not a runtime exploit. The harm is observability:

1. An off-chain accounting system (e.g., the team's own analytics pipeline, a third-party dashboard, a downstream rewards contract) wants to compute 'how many id-4 holders have migrated, and how many id-6 NFTs are migration-origin vs paid-mint-origin'.
2. The only on-chain signals are ClaimBurned (tokenId=4) and ClaimMintedFor (dispatcherIndex=6). The indexer must match (a) same tx hash, (b) ClaimBurned.quantity equals the number of ClaimMintedFor entries with dispatcherIndex=6 and the matching recipient, (c) the ClaimMintedFor minter argument is the pooler address.
3. If the protocol later authorises a second burner of id-4 (e.g., a separate redemption path for unmigrated id-4 holders) or a second minter of id-6 (e.g., a giveaway / promotional mint), the structural match breaks. The indexer silently mis-attributes. Off-chain rewards may pay the wrong cohort.

A single emitted event `Migrated(address indexed caller, address indexed mintRecipient, uint256 amount)` would make the migration first-class and reconstruction trivial.
mainnet_realism_check: Pure observability gap. No AMM dependency. Mainnet indexers are aware of this class of issue (e.g., Uniswap V2 vs V3 event-shape differences) and consistently flag missing first-class events as a maintainability concern.
recommendation: Add a contract-level event: `event Migrated(address indexed caller, address indexed mintRecipient, uint256 amount, uint256 oldNftId, uint256 newNftIndex);` and emit it once at the end of migrateMint. This (a) makes downstream consumers reorg-safe and structurally simple, (b) future-proofs the function against additional authorized burners / minters being added to NFTMinterV2, and (c) makes the intent visible to anyone reading explorer logs.
